\section{1}

\selectlanguage{brazil}%
Suppose we have the operators $A=\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\
1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\
0 & -1
\end{pmatrix}.$ We can verify that they do not commute, since 
\[
[A,B]=AB-BA=\begin{pmatrix}0 & -2\\
2 & 0
\end{pmatrix}\neq0.
\]

For the operator $A$, the eigenvalues are $\left\{ +1,-1\right\} $ with corresponding normalized eigenvectors

\[
|a_{+1}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\
1
\end{pmatrix},\qquad|a_{-1}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}-1\\
1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Suppose, for example, that after measuring $A$, we obtain the value $a=+1$. The system is then in the corresponding eigenstate, $|\psi\rangle=|a_{+1}\rangle.$ Now consider measuring $B$. The eigenvalues of $B$ are also $\left\{ +1,-1\right\} $ with corresponding eigenvectors

\[
|b_{+1}\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}1\\
0
\end{pmatrix},\qquad|b_{-1}\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}0\\
1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The probability of obtaining a particular eigenvalue $b_{n}$ is given by the squared magnitude of the inner product between the corresponding eigenvector and the state of the system: $P(b_{n})=|\langle b_{n}|\psi\rangle|^{2}$. Therefore,

\begin{align*}
P(b_{+1})=|\langle b_{+1}|a_{+1}\rangle|^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\\
P(b_{-1})=|\langle b_{-1}|a_{-1}\rangle|^{2}=\frac{1}{2}
\end{align*}

Thus, there is a $50\%$ probability of observing $+1$ and a $50\%$ probability of observing $-1$. In other words, since $A$ and $B$ do not commute and, in this example, do not share any eigenvectors, after measuring one of the observables, the outcome of a subsequent measurement of the other is intrinsically indeterminate within this mathematical formalism.

\section{1}

Let us consider the operator $A=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 2
\end{pmatrix}.$ To verify that it is a Hermitian matrix, we can verify its conjugate transpose$A^{\dagger}=A.$ Its eigenvalues are $\left\{ 1,1,2\right\} ,$and the corresponding eigenvectors (each column is an eigenvector) are $\left(\left|a_{1}\right\rangle ,\left|a_{2}\right\rangle ,\left|a_{3}\right\rangle \right)=\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.$ We have then that eigenvalue $1$ is degenerate. We can reconstruct matrix $A$ by spectral decomposition: $A=\sum^{3}_{n=1}a_{n}\left|a_{n}\right\rangle \left\langle a_{n}\right|.$ We have now defined a Hermitian matrix $B=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 & 0\\
1 & 4 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 5
\end{pmatrix}.$ We can verify that they commute, that is, $\left[A,B\right]=AB-BA=0$. In the simplest case, we then have a subspace of only one dimension for eigenvalue $2$. We can see that $B\left|a_{3}\right\rangle =5\left|a_{3}\right\rangle $. 

Now for eigenvalue $1$, we have a two-dimensional subspace formed by the vectors $\left\{ \left|a_{1}\right\rangle ,\left|a_{2}\right\rangle \right\} $. All non-null vectors in this subspace continue to be eigenvectors of $A$ with the same eigenvalue $1$, Any non-null vector that is a linear combination of them, $\left|u\right\rangle =a\left|a_{1}\right\rangle +b\left|a_{2}\right\rangle ,$ is also an eigenvector of $A$. In fact,

\[
A\left|u\right\rangle =A\left(a\left|a_{1}\right\rangle +b\left|a_{2}\right\rangle \right)=aA\left|a_{1}\right\rangle +bA\left|a_{2}\right\rangle =a\left(1\cdot\left|a_{1}\right\rangle \right)+b\left(1\cdot\left|a_{2}\right\rangle \right)=a\left|a_{1}\right\rangle +b\left|a_{2}\right\rangle =1\cdot\left|u\right\rangle 
\]

Now applying $B$ to the first eigenvector, we can see that it is a linear combination of the other two vectors in the subspace and is not a $B$ eigenvector:

\[
B\left|a_{1}\right\rangle =\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 & 0\\
1 & 4 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 5
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\
0\\
0
\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\
1\\
0
\end{pmatrix}=3\left|a_{1}\right\rangle +\left|a_{2}\right\rangle 
\]

That is, even though these two eigenvectors associated with $1$ are a basis for this subspace, they do not form a common eigenvector basis. But we can build one. Since all non-null vectors in this subspace are eigenvectors of $A$, we only need to find those who are also eigenvectors of $B$. In this two-dimensional space, $B$'s action on the vectors of the space is given by $B_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}3 & 1\\
1 & 4
\end{pmatrix}.$ Its eigenvalues are $\left\{ 2.38,4.62\right\} $ and the corresponding eigenvectors (each column is an eigenvector) are $\begin{pmatrix}-0.85 & -0.53\\
0.53 & -0.85
\end{pmatrix}.$

Combining with the previous results, we can have a new basis given by the eigenvectors (where each column corresponds to a vector of the new basis)

\[
\left(\left|b_{1}\right\rangle ,\left|b_{2}\right\rangle ,\left|b_{3}\right\rangle \right)=\begin{pmatrix}-0.85 & -0.53 & 0\\
0.53 & -0.85 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

We can test by applying $A$ to the vectors of the new basis:

\begin{align*}
A\left|b_{1}\right\rangle  & =\left|b_{1}\right\rangle  & \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 2
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-0.85\\
0.53\\
0
\end{pmatrix} & =\begin{pmatrix}-0.85\\
0.53\\
0
\end{pmatrix}\\
A\left|b_{2}\right\rangle  & =\left|b_{2}\right\rangle  & \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 2
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-0.53\\
-0.85\\
0
\end{pmatrix} & =\begin{pmatrix}-0.53\\
-0.85\\
0
\end{pmatrix}\\
A\left|b_{3}\right\rangle  & =2\left|b_{3}\right\rangle  & \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 2
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
0\\
1
\end{pmatrix} & =2\begin{pmatrix}0\\
0\\
1
\end{pmatrix}
\end{align*}

We can test by applying $B$ to the vectors of the new basis:

\begin{align*}
B\left|b_{1}\right\rangle  & =2.38\left|b_{1}\right\rangle  & \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 & 0\\
1 & 4 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 5
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-0.85\\
0.53\\
0
\end{pmatrix} & =2.38\begin{pmatrix}-0.85\\
0.53\\
0
\end{pmatrix}\\
B\left|b_{2}\right\rangle  & =4.62\left|b_{2}\right\rangle  & \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 & 0\\
1 & 4 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 5
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}-0.53\\
-0.85\\
0
\end{pmatrix} & =4.62\begin{pmatrix}-0.53\\
-0.85\\
0
\end{pmatrix}\\
B\left|b_{3}\right\rangle  & =5\left|b_{3}\right\rangle  & \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 & 0\\
1 & 4 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 5
\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0\\
0\\
1
\end{pmatrix} & =5\begin{pmatrix}0\\
0\\
1
\end{pmatrix}
\end{align*}
